judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (rank 0, same coordinate) under Sub-Strand 'Measurement- (Perimeter and Area)' but under different Content Standards: B4.3.3.1.3 'Develop and apply a formula for determining perimeter of square and rectangle' (perimeter standard) and B4.3.3.2.1 'Recognise that area is measured in square units' (area standard). They address complementary measurement attributes of the same 2-D shapes: formula-based perimeter computation versus the unit basis for area. This is substantive conceptual coherence within measurement, but neither statement's proficiency is evidenced as supporting success in the other: developing a perimeter formula does not underpin recognising square units, and recognising area units does not underpin perimeter formulas. The lexical 'square' overlap flagged by nomination is coincidental (square shape vs square units) and the shared sub-strand/code prefix alone is not developmental evidence, so a permitted buildsTowards direction is not supported at equal rank. judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, same coordinate) in Strand 1 Number / Sub-strand 1 Counting, Representation & Cardinality, but under different Content Standards: B5.1.1.2.2 asks learners to count and convert Hindu Arabic numbers to Roman numerals up to 100 (C) and vice versa (LCs: convert both directions, count Hindu Arabic numbers to 100), while B5.1.1.1.1 asks learners to model number quantities up to 1,000,000 using graph sheets and multi-base blocks (place-value modelling LC). They are substantively coherent complementary work on representing number quantities in alternative notations/representations within the same sub-strand, reinforcing numeration and cardinality, yet neither is a demonstrable support for the other: Roman-numeral conversion to 100 does not depend on million-scale place-value modelling, and place-value modelling does not depend on Roman numeral notation. With equal grade rank and no substantive evidence of a developmental step, only the symmetric relation is supported; token overlap is limited to stopwords ('and','to','up') and the shared code prefix is weak evidence only. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so absence of further linkage in the excerpt is not proof of absence.

Same-rank direction is justified by substantive extension in the statement text: B5.2.3.1.1 (second) covers only expressing a given problem as an equation with the unknown represented by a letter/variable, while B5.2.3.1.2 (first) contains that same representation step ('represent the problem with an equation', LC 738624a3) plus identifying the unknown and then solving the problem concretely, pictorially or symbolically (LC aa7e4fdb). Proficiency in writing the equation therefore supports success in the fuller identify-represent-solve indicator, giving second_to_first. judgment.rationale: Both are Indicator-grain statements at the same BASIC 5 coordinate (rank 1) under Content Standard B5.1.3.1 (comparing, adding, subtracting, multiplying fractions) in Sub-Strand Number: Fractions, so same-rank direction rests on statement content rather than shared parentage or code prefix. First (B5.1.3.1.1) establishes the core skill of determining equivalent fractions of given fractions; second (B5.1.3.1.3) explicitly 'uses the concept of equivalent fractions' to rewrite fractions to a common denominator in order to add and subtract like fractions (one denominator a multiple of the other), as confirmed by its two Learning Components on addition and subtraction with equivalent fractions. Proficiency in generating equivalent fractions therefore substantively supports success in the applied common-denominator addition/subtraction indicator, which extends the earlier skill to a new operational context. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted items each), but the retained statement text and LCs are sufficient and non-contradictory.
